## Abstract

Satellite observations are essential for global tropospheric ozone monitoring, but their ability to estimate ground-level

ozone remains limited because of weak sensitivity and substantial uncertainty in retrieved ozone near the surface. In 15

this study, we develop new methods for adjusting satellite ozone observations (IASI+GOME2, OMI/MLS, and CrIS)

through chemistry-transport reanalysis and in situ ozone vertical profile measurements. Using these methods, we

create global maps of ground-level ozone concentrations based on satellite observations. We use the Bayesian

Maximum Entropy framework to horizontally interpolate the vertical profiles from ozonesondes and IAGOS and

improve the accuracy of both the satellite column measurements and the surface-to-column ratios from a chemical 20

reanalysis. This is done for monthly average maximum daily 8-hr ozone concentrations over several years. For the

three satellites, surface ozone estimated from the BME-adjusted column-to-surface conversion showed improved

agreement with TOAR-II observations. For IASI+GOME2 (2017-2020), global R2 increased from 0.25 to 0.51, and

RMSE was reduced from 10.74 ppb to 9.44 ppb. For OMI/MLS tropospheric column (2005-2022), global R2 increased

from 0.26 to 0.57, and RMSE decreased from 22.21 ppb to 7.79 ppb. For the CrIS 0-3km ozone (2022), global R2 25

increased from 0.30 to 0.56, and RMSE decreased from 16.48 ppb to 9.45 ppb. The method's efficacy was found to

be highest within 6° of a vertical profile station and most impactful when the original satellite data quality was low.

The resulting satellite-based monthly ground-level ozone estimates can be used further as an independent input to data

fusion methods.

1. Introduction 30

Ozone at ground level is a secondary air pollutant with harmful impacts on human health (Balmes, 2022) and plants

(Mills et al., 2018). Ozone is also a major greenhouse gas, ranking third in its contribution to anthropogenic climate

change behind carbon dioxide and methane (Masson-Delmotte et al., 2021). According to the Global Burden of

Disease 2021 (GBD) study, surface ozone contributed to the deaths of approximately 490,000 (95% UI: 107,000–

837,000) people globally in 2021, accounting for 0.72% (95% UI: 0.16% – 1.18%) of all deaths (Brauer et al., 2024). 35

Recognizing its importance, the Tropospheric Ozone Assessment Report (TOAR) provides the most extensive

compilation of ground-level ozone data by aggregating thousands of monitoring stations worldwide, and its second

phase (TOAR-II) is further expanding coverage in regions like China and India (Schröder et al., 2021; Schultz et al.,

2017). The TOAR dataset enables analysis of ozone distribution and trends (Gaudel et al., 2018). For example,

research using TOAR-II data reveals that in the United States, although extreme ozone concentrations have declined, 40

winter concentrations have actually increased in the Southwest and Midwest regions since the 1990s (Chang et al.,

2025). In contrast, East Asia and Southeast Asia have emerged as current hotspots for ozone pollution, with ozone

concentration significantly exceeding those currently observed in the United States and Europe (Lu et al., 2025). In

densely populated regions of China, such as the North China Plain and the Yangtze River Delta, the upward trend in

ozone concentrations has intensified markedly, with summer seasonal averages in these areas now exceed 75 ppb (Li 45

et al., 2025a). In South America, based on TOAR-II data, trends in ground-level ozone concentrations vary by

geographic location, with high-altitude background monitoring stations exhibiting an upward trend, whereas the

southernmost regions demonstrate a downward trend (Seguel et al., 2024).

Despite significant progress, the limited availability of ground-based monitoring, particularly in developing countries 50

and remote areas, makes it challenging to accurately track surface ozone and fully understand its variations over time

and space. To bridge gaps in regions lacking ground-based ozone monitors, researchers have employed various data

fusion methods, including geostatistical approaches, machine learning, and chemical reanalysis. Geostatistical datasets

fuse ozone observations with composite outputs from multiple chemistry models, leveraging spatial and temporal

autocorrelations (Becker et al., 2023). Machine learning datasets use neural networks to fuse various data sources, 55

including ground-based observations, chemical model outputs, and meteorology (Liu et al., 2022; Sun et al., 2022).

Chemical reanalysis products utilize atmospheric composition from satellite data and have not included ground-level

ozone observations in their data assimilation process (Miyazaki, 2024; Inness et al., 2019). A recent comparison of

six global ground-level ozone datasets reveals significant discrepancies in ozone magnitude, spatial patterns, and

trends, with average estimates differing by as much as 5–10 parts per billion (ppb), while most datasets tend to 60

overestimate ozone at lower concentration (Wang et al., 2025).

Satellite observations have the potential to improve our understanding of the global distribution of ground-level ozone.

Satellite remote sensing offers a distinct advantage in this regard, providing daily, global coverage of tropospheric

ozone overcoming the sparse distribution of other monitoring networks (Yang et al., 2025). Satellite retrievals have 65

been used as a key input for chemical reanalysis products, offering a way to understand ozone column densities, as

well as some machine learning datasets (Hickman et al., 2025; Sekiya et al., 2025). These continuous global records

are important for quantifying long-term trends and understanding the transport of tropospheric ozone (Van Malderen

et al., 2025). However, satellite retrievals can be compromised by biases between different products, instrument drift,

and cloud interference (Pennington et al., 2025). More importantly, these satellite retrievals lack the sensitivity 70

necessary to accurately measure ozone concentrations near the surface, which is the layer most relevant to human

health (Ziemke et al., 2019). To overcome the limited sensitivity of satellite retrievals to near-surface ozone,

multispectral retrieval techniques that synergistically combine measurements from different spectral ranges have been

developed over past years (Mettig et al., 2022). The OMI/MLS product provides tropospheric column ozone using the

Tropospheric Ozone Residual (TOR) technique, which subtracts the stratospheric column ozone measured by the 75

Microwave Limb Sounder (MLS) from the total column ozone measured by the Ozone Monitoring Instrument (OMI)

(Ziemke et al., 2006). IASI+GOME2, a satellite product that couples Thermal Infrared (TIR) radiances from the

Infrared Atmospheric Sounding Interferometer (IASI) and Ultraviolet (UV) reflectance from the Global Ozone

Monitoring Experiment 2 (GOME2), offers insights into the lowermost troposphere (LMT, 0-3 km) and effectively

lowers the altitude of peak sensitivity to around 2.2 km over land (Cuesta et al., 2022; Cuesta et al., 2013). Similarly, 80

the AIRS/OMI product integrates TIR radiances from the Atmospheric Infrared Sounder (AIRS) and UV reflectance

from the OMI to generate vertical profiles capable of distinguishing between upper and lower tropospheric ozone (Fu

et al., 2018). Recently, satellite data from single high-resolution TIR instruments like the Cross-track Infrared Sounder

(CrIS) have been processed using the advanced algorithm MUSES (MUlti-SpEctra, MUlti-SpEcies, MUlti-SEnsors)

to provide a reliable ozone retrieval (Pennington et al., 2025; Fu et al., 2018). 85

To adjust and validate satellite ozone retrievals, researchers rely on high-quality, in-situ vertical profile observations.

Ozonesondes are considered a reference standard due to their high accuracy and fine vertical resolution, making them

essential for correcting satellite data (Gaudel et al., 2024). Similarly, the In-service Aircraft for a Global Observing

System (IAGOS) program utilizes instruments on commercial aircraft to provide high-quality ozone profiles, offering 90

a denser sampling frequency than ozonesondes and valuable data over regions like Asia and Africa that often lack

long-term ozonesonde sites (Wang et al., 2022). While vertical profile observations are valuable for assessing the

performance of satellite products, their utility is constrained by sparse global coverage and low sampling frequency

(typically weekly). These limitations introduce significant uncertainty into long-term records, complicating the

detection of ozone trends (Chang et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2024). Consequently, these vertical profiles cannot be 95

directly applied to correct satellite retrievals of ground-level ozone on a global scale.

Previous studies have integrated ground-based measurements with satellite data to constrain estimates of ground-level

ozone. Xue et al. (2020) utilized random forest models to estimate daily surface ozone across China by combining in

situ observations with chemical transport model simulations (CMAQ) and satellite-derived ozone profiles from the 100

Ozone Monitoring Instrument (OMI), achieving R2 of around 0.70 against ground observations for 2013–2017.

However, machine learning methods usually do not utilize the vertical profile structure to physically derive surface

ozone from the satellite column; instead, they incorporate satellite column ozone within a data-driven model to

estimate ground-level observations (Li and Cheng, 2021). Also, the reliance of machine learning on ground-based

monitors limits its ability to estimate surface ozone before 2013 in China, when the monitoring network was 105

established (Wei et al., 2022). Zhang et al. (2021) developed a deep learning Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)

model to estimate ozone concentrations from the lower stratosphere to near surface by training it on a combination of

ozonesonde profiles, meteorological data (ERA5), and satellite radiances (AIRS/OMI). While the LSTM model

utilized ozonesonde vertical profiles to derive surface ozone from satellite observations,its ability to capture vertical

ozone distributions was limited to the locations of the ozonesonde sites, and their validation of ground-level ozone in 110

China was aggregated into three broad regions (Sichuan Basin, North China Plain, and Yangtze River Delta), without

reporting detailed performance metrics for more locations. Colombi et al. (2021) developed a method to infer surface

ozone from multispectral satellite data (TES/OMI) by integrating surface-to-column ratios from a chemical reanalysis,

and correcting those ratios based on ozonesondes and ground-based observations. While this approach demonstrated

that utilizing vertical information from a chemical reanalysis allows for the effective inference of ground-level ozone 115

from satellite columns, its application is limited to the United States and China during summer (2005–2009) with a 2°

x 2° resolution (Colombi et al., 2021). Furthermore, the method relied on spatially uniform bias corrections over broad

regions, which did not to account for how satellite ozone and vertical ozone profile estimates are biased in nonlinear

and spatially heterogeneous ways. While recent methods have increasingly attempted to leverage vertical information,

they remain constrained by their reliance on ground-based observations for training or bias correction, which restricts 120

their application to specific regions and time periods.

In this study, we attempt to improve global surface ozone estimates from satellites by developing a geostatistical

framework for adjusting the column to surface conversion that effectively propagates vertical profile information

across the horizontal domain. Unlike the spatially uniform corrections employed by Colombi et al. (2021), our method 125

utilizes the Bayesian Maximum Entropy (BME) method to correct nonlinear and regionally varying biases in both the

satellite ozone column concentrations and the chemical reanalysis surface-to-column ratios. By applying a BME

adjustment, our study propagates these corrections smoothly in space based on the spatial autocorrelation of monthly

fitted ozonesonde and IAGOS observations. We apply this BME-adjusted column to surface conversion framework

to three different satellite datasets to estimate monthly global ground-level ozone, over the years for which these 130

satellite data are available from 2005 to 2022. The three satellite datasets are IASI+GOME2 0-3 km ozone (Cuesta et

al., 2013; Cuesta et al., 2022), OMI/MLS tropospheric column ozone (Ziemke et al., 2006), and CrIS 0-3 km or

tropospheric column ozone (Bowman, 2022). The BME-adjusted surface ozone estimates allow us to infer global

surface monthly mean Daily Maximum 8-Hour Average (DMA8) ozone at a 1° × 1° resolution over multiple years.

We selected the monthly mean DMA8 for this study as it is widely used in health-related research, effectively 135

capturing both the ozone seasonal cycle and the burden of ground-level exposure (Fleming et al., 2018). Our estimates

are evaluated against independent ground observations from TOAR-II and benchmarked against the original satellite

measurements and the Tropospheric Chemistry Reanalysis Version 2 (TCR-2) surface ozone. By intentionally

excluding ground-based observations from the adjustment process, we ensure that our satellite-based product serves

as an independent input for future data fusion studies. 140

vertical profiles from ozonesonde and IAGOS observations. While we focus on the monthly average DMA8 because

### 2.1 Satellite data

IASI+GOME2 uses multispectral retrieval techniques derived from the combined radiances in the TIR detected by

IASI and UV measured by GOME2 (synergism of level 1 radiance measurements). Both instruments are aboard on

the MetOp satellites, providing daily global coverage at a ground resolution of approximately 12 km diameter pixels 150

at the satellite overpass time around 9:30 AM local time (Cuesta et al., 2013). The IASI+GOME2 multispectral

approach is specifically designed to enhance sensitivity to ozone from the surface up to 3 km altitude, where single

retrievals from either TIR or UV instruments have limited sensitivity. For this, it combines information from the two

spectral domains and optimizes it through altitude dependent Phillips-Tikhonov type constraints. Degrees of Freedom

(DOF) represent the number of independent vertical structures that can be resolved by the satellite measurement, 155

which is calculated as the trace of the averaging kernel matrix (Colombi et al., 2021). While IASI and GOME2 each

typically provide 3.3 DOF for the entire atmosphere, IASI+GOME2 improves to 5 DOF for the entire atmosphere

(accounting for approximately 1.6 DOF for tropospheric ozone) in average (Cuesta et al., 2013). IASI+GOME2 has

been validated against ozonesondes at multiple locations (46 stations distributed worldwide) with a total of 1035

records, demonstrating good agreement in the lowermost troposphere with a high correlation (R = 0.85) (Cuesta et al., 160

2018). In this study, we use monthly average 0-3 km ozone obtained from daily IASI+GOME2 observations at

approximately 9:30 AM local time overpass from 2017 to 2020 at 1° x 1° resolution.

The OMI/MLS tropospheric column ozone product is derived using the TOR technique, which subtracts the

stratospheric column ozone measured by MLS from the total column ozone measured by OMI. A key advantage of 165

this product is that both instruments are on the NASA Aura satellite (1:45 PM overpass), resulting in a more reliable

estimate of tropospheric ozone (Ziemke et al., 2006). Characterized by a standard deviation (random uncertainty) of

approximately 1.3 Dobson Units (DU) for monthly observations, the OMI/MLS dataset has proven robust for

assessing seasonal and long-term atmospheric changes (Elshorbany et al., 2024; Fadnavis et al., 2025). In this study,

we use OMI/MLS monthly tropospheric column ozone at 1° x 1° resolution from 2005 to 2022 (Ziemke et al., 2006), 170

with the tropopause defined by the thermal tropopause from National Centers for Environmental Prediction (NCEP)

reanalysis data.

Unlike multispectral products such as IASI+GOME2 and OMI/MLS, CrIS is a lower noise TIR instrument aboard the

Suomi-NPP satellite launched in 2011 (1:30 PM overpass) whose data are processed using the MUSES algorithm with 175

a spatial resolution of 14 km (Fu et al., 2018; Mettig et al., 2022). While CrIS provides high spectral resolution, its

vertical sensitivity is physically constrained by limited thermal contrast, resulting in lower sensitivity in the lower

troposphere compared to the upper troposphere. Validation indicates that the Tropospheric Ozone and its Precursors

from Earth System Sounding (TROPESS) CrIS product generally exhibits a positive bias in the tropospheric column

(4.8%) relative to ozonesondes (Pennington et al., 2025). This study uses the CrIS L2 Ozone forward stream product 180

for 2022, which provides 26 vertical layers (from the surface to 0.1 hPa) and approximately 23,569 targets per day

2.2 Ozone vertical profile observations 185

Ozonesondes provide high quality vertical profile observations of ozone from the surface into the stratosphere. The

instruments are launched on balloons and measure ozone partial pressure with a high vertical resolution of

approximately 100 m. However, these datasets are limited by a low sampling frequency (often weekly or less).

Furthermore, their long-term data records often require complex homogenization to correct for instrumental changes

over years and may exhibit biases at high altitudes (Ancellet et al., 2022). To address the latter issue, this study uses 190

the homogenized ozonesonde time series from the TOAR-II Harmonization and Evaluation of Ground-based

Instruments for Free-Tropospheric Ozone Measurements (HEGIFTOM) working group, which corrects for

instrumental and processing biases to reduce uncertainty for sites across global networks like Southern Hemisphere

Additional Ozonesondes (SHADOZ) and the World Ozone and Ultraviolet Radiation Data Centre (WOUDC) (Smit

and Thompson, 2021; Van Malderen et al., 2025). For this study, we utilize 36 ozonesonde locations from 195

HEGIFTOM and 8 from WOUDC, selecting only those with a minimum of six qualifying months (defined as months

having at least four measurements) over 2005 to 2022 (list of sites can be found in Table S1).

IAGOS provides vertical ozone profiles from instruments on commercial passenger aircraft as they take off and land,

which has greater sampling frequency than ozonesondes, but its observations are unevenly distributed, with dense 200

coverage over Europe and North America but sparse sampling in the Southern Hemisphere and other remote regions

(Gaudel et al., 2020). In addition, since the IAGOS program relies on commercial flight routes, near-surface data are

largely restricted to airport vicinities where local airport and urban emissions may limit their spatial representativeness

and relevance for general population exposure assessments (Petetin et al., 2016; Gaudel et al., 2018). Therefore, we

only use the IAGOS data above 200 m to limit the influence of local airport emissions. For this study, we include 48 205

IAGOS locations where vertical profiles were measured during aircraft ascent and descent near major airports. These

airports were selected using the same standards as the ozonesondes (list of airports can be found in Table S1).

### 2.3 Chemical reanalysis

TCR-2 is generated by assimilating satellite observations of ozone, CO, NO2, HNO3 and SO2 from satellite instruments

such as OMI, MLS and MOPITT into the MIROC-Chem model (Miyazaki et al., 2020a). In situ surface observations

were not included in the data assimilation. When compared to worldwide ozonesonde measurements in the lower 225

troposphere (up to 500 hPa), TCR-2 shows a low bias among world regions of -0.4 to 4.2 ppb (Miyazaki et al., 2020b).

This study uses TCR-2 2-hourly ozone profiles from 9-11 am and 12-2 pm at a 1.125° x 1.125° resolution, where 9-

11 am is intended to correspond to the overpass time of IASI+GOME2, and 12-2 pm to the overpass time of OMI/MLS

and CrIS. Details on the input satellite data used in data assimilation of TCR-2 are summarized in Table S2.

2.4 Ground-level ozone observations 230

For evaluation, we use the latest TOAR-II ground-based observation dataset from 2005 to 2022, focusing on monthly

mean DMA8 ozone. Building on TOAR-I (Schultz et al., 2017), TOAR-II represents the most extensive collection of

global tropospheric ozone measurements, incorporating an expanded dataset that notably includes monitoring data

from approximately 1,400 stations across China after 2015 (https://toar-data.fz-juelich.de/gui/v2/dashboard/, last

access: 20 May 2025) (Schröder et al., 2021). As TOAR-II observations for the United States are only available 235

through spring 2022, the observation dataset is supplemented with observations from the US EPA Air Quality System

(AQS) for the remainder of 2022. We process the ground-based observations using a 75% data recording threshold,

calculating a monthly mean only if a station reported valid DMA8 ozone values for at least 75% of the days that month.

Due to the detection of possible incorrect units, we have removed all France data in 2014 (Wang et al., 2025). The

total number of stations used in our evaluation that met this standard varied from a minimum of 3,355 in January 2005 240

to a peak of 7,073 in June 2022. The spatial distribution of monitoring stations and their proximity to the nearest

vertical profiles is shown in Fig. 1(c), with more yearly maps available in Figure S1.

### 3.1 Monthly trend of vertical profiles

To improve the reliability of our analysis, we calculate the monthly fitted value of vertical ozone profiles from daily

observations of 44 ozonesonde and 48 IAGOS sites globally. While ozonesondes offer highly accurate data, their low 255

sampling frequency (typically once a week) can create a significant bias when calculating monthly averages.

Approximating a monthly mean from only four measurements can lead to an error of about 4 ppb (10%) (Chang et al.,

2024). Following Chang et al. (2025), we applied a Generalized Additive Model (GAM) to calculate the monthly

fitted value for both the 0-3 km and the tropospheric column ozone with respect to its seasonal and interannual changes.

The specific equation used to derive these values is: 260

𝑦(𝑡, ℎ) = 𝑓𝑠𝑒𝑎𝑠𝑜𝑛(𝑚, ℎ) + 𝑓𝑖𝑛𝑑𝑒𝑥(𝑡, ℎ) + 𝑒𝑟𝑟𝑜𝑟  (2)

where ℎ represents altitude, grouped into 100 m vertical bins from the surface to the top of the troposphere (for IAGOS

data, only measurements above 200 m are used to avoid unusual ground-level measurements near airports); 𝑚 265

represents the month (1-12); 𝑡 is a continuous monthly index for all years with valid observations (N_years) at each

site where 𝑡 = 1, ..., 12 x N_years; and 𝑓 is the basic function, for which we use Duchon splines. After filtering the

data, we aggregate the ozone concentrations by altitude, month and year. The GAM above is then used to fit the

aggregated data, allowing us to generate a continuous, monthly fitted vertical ozone profile at a 100 m resolution over

years covered for each site. Examples of the resulting fitted time series are shown in Figure S2. 270

### 3.2 Filtering and Preprocessing Input Data

Data preprocessing aimed to standardize datasets including satellite products, TCR-2 and TOAR-II observations to a

common 1° x 1° resolution and monthly scale. This began with a filtering stage to ensure input data quality. For

IASI+GOME2 and CrIS, we retained 0–3 km column ozone data only if the DOF exceeded 0.2. For IASI+GOME2

and OMI/MLS, we removed the data if cloud reflectivity was more than 0.30. For the CrIS dataset, we filtered for grid 275

grid cells from CrIS and TCR-2 where the surface pressure was below 700 hPa or surface height is over 3000 m before

proceeding with 0-3 km column ozone calculations.

### 3.3 BME data fusion and column to surface conversion

We employ the Bayesian Maximum Entropy (BME) framework, a geostatistical data fusion method that produces

estimates of a homogeneous, stationary, space random field by integrating multiple forms of knowledge (Serre and

Christakos, 1999; Christakos et al., 2004; Christakos, 1990). Prior to applying the BME framework, we evaluated the 300

statistical distributions of all 0-3 km ozone, tropospheric column ozone and ratio datasets to verify the Gaussian

assumption inherent to geostatistical estimation. As illustrated in Figure S4, the 0–3 km ozone concentrations, surface-

to-column ratios (0–3 km), and tropospheric column ozone concentrations exhibited approximate normality and were

### 3.4 Evaluation of derived surface ozone with TOAR-II ground observations

We evaluate the derived surface ozone fields with respect to monthly average DMA8 ozone TOAR-II observations

(2005–2022). The primary metrics for evaluation are the coefficient of determination (R²) and root mean square error 410

(RMSE), which are analyzed across different seasons and regions. For comparison, we evaluate the performance of

different datasets against TOAR-II observations over a common temporal range: (1) the original satellite observations

(monthly average), (2) TCR-2 (monthly average DMA8), and (3) our final BME-adjusted surface ozone (monthly

average DMA8). We quantify the BME-adjusted conversion method against the conversion method without the BME

adjustment process (only using the TCR2 ratio directly in Equation 1), focusing on the distance from a given TOAR- 415

II grid cell to the nearest vertical profile location. Furthermore, we conduct an analysis to investigate how indicators

of satellite observation quality for IASI+GOME2 impact the final derived surface ozone estimates.

For the surface ozone derived from OMI/MLS, we also perform a long-term trend evaluation against TOAR-II trends

from 2005 to 2022, using area-weighted ozone means. Prior to trend estimation, we deseasonalize the time series to 420

remove the influence of the seasonal cycle, consistent with TOAR-II recommendations. The seasonal signal is

modeled using four harmonic terms based on monthly data from 2005 to 2022 (Supporting Information Section S2).

After removing the seasonal signal for each region, trends are calculated using median quantile regression, and the

confidence in each trend was classified by its p-value: very high (p ≤ 0.01), high (0.01 < p ≤ 0.05), medium (0.05 < p

≤ 0.1), low (0.1 < p ≤ 0.33), or no evidence (p > 0.33). Additionally, the 95% confidence interval (CI) for each dataset 425

was determined through a linear regression against the gridded TOAR-II observations. We use regional groupings

defined by Hemispheric Transport Air Pollution 2 (HTAP2) (Koffi et al., 2016), as detailed in Table S3.

## 5. Discussion

The validation results in Table 2 demonstrate that the BME-adjusted conversion method significantly improves surface

ozone estimation from satellite data. This performance enhancement is driven by the use of observed vertical profiles

to adjust the surface-to-column ratio from TCR-2 and column ozone observations from the satellites. The surface-to-

column ratio effectively characterizes key physical processes such as boundary layer mixing and photochemical 590

production (Colombi et al., 2021). Specifically, a high ratio implies strong near-surface photochemical production

coupled with a stable boundary layer that traps ozone near the ground. Conversely, a low ratio indicates vertical mixing

or convective transport that moves ozone concentrations into the free troposphere. The vertical profile observations

of column ozone also play a critical role by reducing systematic errors in the satellite column observations (0–3 km

and tropospheric). By fusing these fitted monthly vertical profiles from ozonesondes and IAGOS, the BME framework 595

removes spatially varying retrieval biases, which arise from the sensor or a priori assumptions. Thus, the final derived

surface ozone estimates benefit from the surface-to-column ratio conversion, which constrains vertical distribution

physics, and the column ozone adjustment, which calibrates the magnitude of the ozone concentration.

The spatial maps (Fig. 3 and Fig. 4) and validation metrics (Table 2) reveal crucial insights in how the BME adjustment 600

interacts with satellite products. For tropospheric column products, which exhibit a weak correlation with surface

ozone due to the integration of the full tropospheric column, the BME adjustments yields significant improvements

globally. However, for the 0–3 km ozone products, which have better sensitivity to the lower atmosphere, the efficacy

of the adjustment is not uniform spatially. The pronounced regional heterogeneity in adjustment performance

highlights the BME method's dependence on three types of input data: the quality of the original satellite retrieval, the 605

density of the vertical profile network, and the surface-to-column ratio accuracy of the chemical reanalysis. In the

United States and Europe, the method achieves its highest performance gains despite the large biases in the original

satellite data. This success is driven by the dense network of vertical profile observations, which allows the BME

framework to effectively model the local spatial covariance structure and constrain the satellite retrieval. In contrast,

regions with sparse vertical profiles observations (like China) depend heavily on the TCR-2 ratio, since the spatial 610

correlation of the surface-to-column ratio decays rapidly. However, when this reanalysis uncertainty interacts with

original satellite data, the BME-adjusted conversion effectively introduces bias, explaining the performance

degradation observed in some regions (like Japan, South Korean).

As noted by Colombi et al. (2021), the combination of high surface temperatures (critical for TIR sensors) and high 615

solar elevation angles (critical for UV sensors) maximize the DOF for signal in the retrieval.  However, summer also

has active photochemical production, which introduces high ozone concentrations and complex vertical mixing

profiles that are challenging to model. Consequently, even though satellite datasets perform well in R2, they still have

larger bias during this season. In contrast, winter observations are often constrained by low thermal contrast, causing

the satellite retrieval to rely heavily on a priori information rather than the actual ozone concentration (Pennington et 620

al., 2025). While the signal is naturally lower in winter due to lower background ozone concentrations, the relative

improvement provided by the BME-adjusted conversion is more pronounced than in summer. Another consistent

pattern observed in Fig. 7 is that derived surface ozone performs better in rural areas than in urban areas for all satellite

products. This disparity is likely driven by representativeness errors associated with the original satellite data. Rural

ozone concentrations are more spatially uniform, meaning that a single satellite pixel can better represent a broad area., 625

while urban environments tend to exhibit sharper ozone gradients over short distances.

The uncertainty maps (in Figure S8) of BME-adjusted surface ozone reflect uncertainties from three primary inputs:

the original satellite retrieval data, the chemical reanalysis (TCR-2), and the vertical ozone profile. The satellite data

quality is linked to the information content of the satellite retrieval. In low information scenarios, when characterized 630

by low DOF for the signal, satellite retrievals largely revert to the a priori climatology, resulting in a lack of

independent sensitivity to real surface ozone variability. Although the LMT (0-3 km) product is theoretically better

able to measure near-surface ozone, performance disparities suggest this advantage is often compromised by the

critical influence of sampling time. In Fig. 5, we found that data fusion-based estimate of surface ozone using

OMI/MLS tropospheric columns and IASI+GOME2 LMT show similar results for both correlation and bias (it is 635

slightly better using the OMI/MLS, although the period of comparison is not the same). It is worth noting that

OMI/MLS measurements around 1:45 PM local time likely capture the daily photochemical peak, and would be

expected to correspond well with daily DMA8 ozone. On the other hand, IASI+GOME2 measurements around 9:30

AM capture the rapid morning transition period, which may be less correlated with DMA8. In Fig. 6, our BME-

adjusted conversion method robustly enhances performance amidst year-to-year variations, effectively smoothing out 640

the interannual fluctuations present in the original satellite datasets.

Although the chemical reanalysis (TCR-2) provides crucial surface-to-column ratios in our method, it still contains

errors. As shown in Fig.7, TCR-2 overestimates surface ozone concentrations. However, our methodology mitigates

this by utilizing the surface-to-column ratio rather than the absolute concentration as the input. This strategy rests on 645

the premise that even if the reanalysis model possesses a bias in magnitude, its simulation of the atmospheric vertical

structure may remain relatively reliable (Colombi et al., 2021). The ratio-based conversion is also applicable to the

retrieval of other air pollutants (Malings et al., 2024). Another source of uncertainty arises from the temporal

representativeness of the vertical profiles. Ozonesonde observations are typically taken at irregular and sparse intervals

throughout the week. Although daily homogenized ozonesonde observations are precise, calculating monthly means 650

from sparse daily observations introduces under-coverage bias due to the high inter-daily variability of free

## 6. Conclusion

This study represents the first global application of a geostatistical framework to estimate ground-level ozone based

on multiple satellite ozone datasets, effectively leveraging vertical profile observations from ozonesondes and IAGOS,

alongside the surface-to-column ratio from a chemical reanalysis (TCR-2). Our global validation against TOAR-II

observations demonstrates that the BME-adjusted conversion method significantly improves the accuracy of surface 665

ozone estimates from OMI/MLS, IASI+GOME2, and CrIS satellite products. The success of this approach is driven

by dual adjustments to the surface-to-column ratio to constrain vertical distribution physics, and to the satellite

observations to reduce systematic biases in the satellite column magnitude. In contrast to purely data-driven machine

learning approaches (e.g., Xue et al., 2020; Wei et al., 2022), which often treat the atmosphere as a 2D surface and

rely heavily on dense ground monitoring networks for training, our method integrates a physics-based vertical 670

constraint via the surface-to-column ratio conversion. Another key advantage of our approach is the use of spatial

autocorrelation with vertical profile observations to weight corrections; this allows the BME framework to capture

non-linearities and heterogeneous bias structures that uniform regional corrections may miss, and to smoothly apply

these corrections spatially. Furthermore, unlike previous studies restricted to specific regions, temporal scales, or data

from a single satellite, we established a robust framework for correcting multiple satellite datasets over long-term 675

periods on a global scale.

Our analysis shows that vertical profile observations exert the most significant corrective influence on spatial

correlation (R2) when satellite measurements are within 6° radius. In contrast, for systematic bias (RMSE), the

adjustment range is considerably larger. Even where vertical profile data are sparse, the method remains highly 680

effective at reducing the satellite retrieval bias, particularly evident in the widespread improvement of RMSE. By

demonstrating this capacity to correct surface ozone estimates, this study extends the utility of these vertical profile

datasets beyond their traditional applications in tropospheric ozone trend analysis. Another innovation is the complete

exclusion of ground monitoring station data from the adjustment process. While previous approaches often assimilated

ground observations to improve local accuracy, this can bias models toward data-rich regions. By relying exclusively 685

on sparse vertical profiles for reducing biases, our method generates an independent satellite-based surface ozone

product.

Despite these achievements, several limitations persist. The method's adjustment and conversion are limited by the

spatiotemporal density of the vertical profile observations and the quality of chemical reanalysis. Therefore, it offers 690

minimal benefits in regions where vertical profiles are few and chemical reanalysis performance is poor. Furthermore,

temporal variations in the magnitude of bias correction across months and years can mathematically mask underlying

physical trends. Even after adjustment, persistent biases remain in satellite-derived products. These residuals stem

from inherent satellite data uncertainties, the inability of chemical reanalysis surface-to-column ratios to fully capture

vertical distributions, and the lack of vertical profile observations in many regions. Consequently, these results 695

underscore the need for increasing observations of ozone vertical profiles.  In summary, the BME-adjusted surface

ozone offers a unique, independent estimate derived from satellite observations. We show that it performs comparably

with a chemical reanalysis, but not as good as ground-level ozone datasets that are currently available.  Its primary

value therefore lies not as a global 'best estimate,' but as a background field based on satellite data for use in future

data fusion frameworks and global air quality assessments particularly in monitor-sparse regions. 700
